il_holy_boulders_and_surrounding.blurb: A bouldering-focused zone in southern Jackson County, Illinois, within Shawnee National Forest country. Almost everything here is a boulder problem, with only a handful of hard sport lines on the side. Difficulty runs from V0 all the way to V12, though most problems sit between V1 and V5, backed by a healthy group of V7s and a few much harder ones. The main Holy Boulders themselves are fine-grained gray sandstone. Most of the climbing in this grouping is on the Hagler Road cluster, a spread of boulders just north of the Holys, while The Hellhole is a small outlier. It suits a dedicated bouldering trip more than a day with a rope.

nj_bouldering_north_central_nj.blurb: Boulder fields scattered across Morris County and most of Passaic County in north central New Jersey, between Interstate 80 and Route 23. Nearly everything is a boulder problem, with just a few top-rope lines. Grades lean easy to moderate, mostly V0 to V5, with a thin tail of harder problems reaching V11. The rock is granite and gneiss around the Ramapo area, while the Green Pond Mountain ridges hold purple-tinted quartzite conglomerate. At Pyramid Mountain the blocks are erratics, outcrops and short cliff bands, with slabs, cracks, overhangs and a few highballs. It is a patchwork of small venues rather than one big crag; the largest are Pyramid Mountain, Norvin Green State Forest, Mountainside Park and Kincaid Woods.

ca_queen_mountain.blurb: Queen Mountain sits in the Queen Valley part of Joshua Tree National Park, at roughly 5,200 feet, in a wilder and more remote corner than the busy central park. Walk-ins here are among the longer ones in the park. Roughly equal parts trad and bouldering, with a few sport routes. Trad routes cluster in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, with some easier lines below and a handful of 5.12s above, while the boulder problems are mostly easy, up to about V5. The rock quality is excellent, with some of the best varnished faces in the park. The biggest sub-areas are Queen Mountain Base, The Underground, Walt's Rocks and the Cirque of the Climbables.

co_cathedral_spires_area.blurb: A cluster of granite spires, pinnacles and buttresses in Colorado's South Platte country, at around 7,400 feet. Trad climbing dominates, with cracks, chimneys, offwidths, slabs and faces, from single-pitch cragging to multipitch. There is also a good dose of bouldering, plus a few sport routes. Trad grades run from 5.7 to 5.13, but the heart of it is 5.10 and 5.11, with a decent number of 5.12s. Most routes face south, so summer can be hot, while fall and winter are the favoured seasons, especially when it is too cold for alpine objectives. The biggest sections are Sunshine Wall, Cynical Pinnacle, The Dome and Snake Buttress.

me_b_southern_coast.blurb: Maine's southern coast runs from South Portland to the New Hampshire border, with rolling interior hills, long sand beaches and old mill towns. Climbing here is mostly bouldering, with some top-rope lines, a few trad routes and the odd ice flow. Problems run from the very easy to about V10, with most between V0 and V4. The largest venues are Kenyon Hill Preserve, Clifford Park, Orris Falls and Nubble Lighthouse. Clifford Park sits on granite from two veins and was quarried long ago, leaving blocky slabs; lichen is common, and early spring and late fall are the preferred times there to dodge the bugs.

wi_niagara_escarpment_kettle_moraine.blurb: The cliffs and boulders of the Niagara Escarpment as it turns south from Door County toward Horicon Marsh in eastern Wisconsin. Bouldering dominates, with a smaller mix of top-rope and trad lines and a couple of ice climbs. Problems mostly run from V0 to V5, topping out around V7, while the roped routes span 5.4 to 5.12. Most of the climbing is at High Cliff State Park on the east shore of Lake Winnebago, where the west-facing cliff is roughly 20 to 35 feet tall with cracks, ledges and some overhanging sections; cracks can stay wet and muddy early in the season. Other spots include Horicon, Jake's Rock and Cave Point in Door County.
